extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, research institutions, funders, and researchers considering adopting transparent (open) peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for journals, publishers, and research stakeholders on designing, piloting, and operating transparent (open) peer review models, and for authors/reviewers participating in such models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of transparent (open) peer review and model types
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review is an umbrella term covering multiple practices that alter traditional anonymous review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish traditional models (single‑blind, double‑blind; reports and decision letters confidential) from transparent/open models: open reports (publish review reports, editor decisions, and author responses with the article; reviewer identity may remain anonymous), open identities (disclose reviewers’ names to authors/readers), and open participation / post‑publication review (community contributes reviews or comments on preprints or published versions). Choose which element(s) of 'openness' to adopt rather than treating transparency as binary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing review reports and responses makes editorial choices and reviewer critiques visible to readers, which can increase trust in editorial decisions and help readers assess the robustness of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame transparency as a way to 'open the black box' of evaluation; consider how published materials help readers assess claims and editorial decisions. Ensure review files are curated and linked clearly so they actually improve trust rather than confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recognition and credit
rubrics_metrics.description: When review reports are citable (for example with DOIs) and traceable to ORCID or reviewer‑recognition platforms, review work becomes visible scholarly contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign DOIs to peer‑review components, integrate ORCID and reviewer‑credit services, and provide metadata so review activity can be counted in assessments and CVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and reproducibility benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Published review histories serve as educational resources for early‑career researchers and can document methodological or reporting gaps addressed during revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use published review histories to support reproducibility and learning; ensure review files are readable and structured to be useful as training materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the evidence base and stakeholder attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence base on transparent review outcomes is growing but mixed, with uncertainties about review quality, reviewer behavior, and acceptance rates; stakeholder surveys show stronger support for publishing reports than revealing reviewer identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review systematic reviews, trials, and pilot data relevant to your discipline before selecting a model; expect variation by field and by the specific practice (reports vs identities vs participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a pilot and clear choice architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a pilot (phased pilots used by Wiley and others) and offer opt‑in or opt‑out options (or test automatic opt‑in with opt‑out) while monitoring uptake and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the pilot to track relevant metrics (opt‑in rates, reviewer declines, editorial workload). Use phased rollouts to refine workflows and messaging. Make the choice architecture explicit and easy to understand for authors and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve reviewer choice where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow reviewers to remain anonymous or to sign reports voluntarily; consider disciplinary norms because some fields are more comfortable with signed review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If identity disclosure is optional, provide clear options and explain implications. Preserve anonymity options to avoid deterring reviewers, especially junior or vulnerable scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign persistent identifiers and integrate recognition systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide persistent identifiers (DOIs) for review reports and support linking to ORCID and reviewer‑credit platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable citable review outputs to make peer review countable and to facilitate credit and recognition in assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create metadata and archiving workflows (machine‑readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make review content machine‑readable and provide metadata and archiving to enable secondary research and support altmetrics and assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop standards for metadata, archiving, and indexing of review files; consider annotation projects that reuse reviews for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train editors and reviewers on tone, confidentiality, and sensitive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide guidance on constructive criticism, confidentiality, and handling sensitive material (e.g., clinical data, dual‑use content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer training modules or guidance documents for editors/reviewers on writing public‑facing reports, redaction policies, and how to flag content that must not be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update institutional and funder assessment frameworks to recognize peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and funders should recognize peer‑review activity (signed or anonymized) and incorporation of review reports in promotion and grant evaluations where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise promotion/panels/grant evaluation criteria to accept citable review outputs and documented review service as evidence of scholarly contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support reviewer training and incentives to broaden reviewer pools
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider small honoraria, formal recognition, or reviewer‑development programs to address workload and geographic disparities in reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement incentives and training to reduce reviewer fatigue and to diversify the reviewer pool (e.g., honoraria, formal recognition programs, reviewer‑development workshops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author preparation for published review files
rubrics_metrics.description: When opting into publishing the peer‑review file, prepare a concise author response and keep revision records clear because these materials become part of the public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clear, concise author responses that document how critiques were addressed and transparently note remaining limitations to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conduct and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: If you sign reviews, focus on constructive, evidence‑based critique; if anonymous while the report is published, ensure reports do not contain identifying or defamatory material and that conflicts of interest are declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reviewers to consider partial disclosure options (e.g., link to a public reviewer profile like ORCID) and to avoid content that could reveal identity. Require COI declarations for published reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and mitigate low reviewer participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory identity disclosure can increase declination rates; plan for higher decline rates and mitigate by offering anonymity and formal recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer optional signing or opt‑out designs, recognize review work formally, and monitor declination patterns during pilots to adjust policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid token transparency—set curation and quality standards for review files
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing reports without curation or standards can confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop guidelines for what review files should include, how they will be edited/redacted/linked to the article, and who is responsible for moderation so published files are useful and comprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and guard against inequitable impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity disclosure may disproportionately affect junior researchers and reviewers from under‑represented regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include safeguards (e.g., optional anonymity, monitoring for differential effects), track participation by career stage and geography, and adjust policy to reduce inequitable burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect legal and ethical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there are legal or ethical constraints (patient data, sensitive security issues), restrict the scope of what becomes public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish redaction and exclusion policies for material that cannot or should not be published; consult legal/privacy experts when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure editorial capacity to moderate and redact content
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must have the capacity to moderate published reports and redact sensitive content before launching transparent review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial resources and workflows; if capacity is lacking, build moderation and redaction processes prior to publishing review histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key metrics to measure during and after a pilot
rubrics_metrics.description: Track quantitative and qualitative indicators such as author opt‑in rate, reviewer sign‑up rate, reviewer decline rate, turnaround time, editorial workload, and reader engagement; collect qualitative feedback and monitor abuse or harassment cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define measurement plan up front: capture both uptake and impact metrics (downloads, citations of review files), collect stakeholder feedback, and have remediation paths for abuse/harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and community fit for adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide to adopt transparent review if your research community values openness and educational benefit; if so, an opt‑in or opt‑out open‑reports model may work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider community norms, legal/ethical constraints, and editorial capacity; adopt iterative approach—pilot, evaluate, protect vulnerable participants, and scale practices that improve trust, training, and reproducibility.
